Each verb that opens a mathematical statement tells the reader what kind of statement follows.
Use each verb only for its own job:

- "Let" introduces a new object,
  as in "let $\predvar$ be an input value".
  It can carry a constraint on that new object,
  as in "let $x \neq 2$".
- "Suppose" or "assume" states a condition on objects already introduced,
  a condition that could fail and that the result depends on,
  as in "assume that $\Sigma$ is positive definite".
- "By", followed by its source, states a consequence of what is already established,
  as in "by [linearity of expectation](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#thm-linearity-expectation), $\E{X + Y} = \E{X} + \E{Y}$".
- "Denote" names notation for an object described in words,
  as in "let $\predval$ denote the prediction"
  or "$\predval$ denotes the prediction".

A "let" in front of a consequence presents a fact as a choice.
The reader then has to work out whether the equation is a definition, a new assumption,
or a result that follows from earlier definitions.
Name the source with "by" instead,
so the reader can check the step.

::: {#exm-by-not-let}

## Stating a consequence with "by"

> ❌ Choose an input value $\predvar$,
> and let the output variable $\Outvar = \truemeanf{\predvar} + \noise$.
>
> ✅ Choose an input value $\predvar$.
> By the definition of the noise $\noise \eqdef \Outvar - \truemeanf{\predvar}$,
> the output variable $\Outvar$ equals $\truemeanf{\predvar} + \noise$.

The ❌ sentence appeared in an earlier version of this guide,
in the [Random variables and their values](#random-variables-and-their-values) section.
The "let" in the ❌ sentence suggests that the equation is an assumption about the output variable.
The noise is defined as the output variable minus its mean,
so the equation follows from that definition,
as the [Guidelines for defining terms](defining-terms.qmd#guidelines-for-defining-terms) section asks of a statistical model.
The ✅ sentence names that definition as the source.

:::

Use "denote", not "write", to name notation.
"Write" names the physical act of putting marks on a page,
and "write $X$ in terms of $Y$" already means "express", <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted idiom, not the defined term -->
as the [Use literal language](inclusive-writing.qmd#use-literal-language) section explains.
"Denote" names the relation between a symbol and the object that the symbol stands for.

::: {#exm-denote-not-write}

## Naming notation with "denote"

> ❌ Choose the number of features before fitting the network.
> Write $L$ for that number.
>
> ✅ Choose the number of features before fitting the network.
> Let $L$ denote that number.

The ❌ sentence adapts a passage of the lab's notes on neural networks.
The "write" in the ❌ sentence reads as an instruction to the reader,
although the sentence only names a symbol.

:::

The `check-avoided-words` check in gha flags "write $X$ for", "writing $X$ for", and "is written $X$" on the lines that a pull request adds.
No check can tell a consequence from an assumption,
because the answer depends on what the text has already defined,
so a reviewer reads for the "let" and "suppose" rules.
